subject: Pathology
summary: Congestive heart failure is the heart’s inability to supply adequate output, often due to systolic, diastolic, or high‑output dysfunction. It presents with pulmonary congestion and systemic venous stasis, and requires rapid assessment of cause and severity.

sections.p: CHF occurs when cardiac output falls below metabolic needs or when filling pressures rise, leading to pulmonary and systemic congestion. Diagnosis combines clinical signs, BNP/NT‑proBNP, and imaging.
b: Heart cannot meet metabolic demand or does so at high filling pressures

t.b: Elevated BNP indicates ventricular stretch; >125 pg/mL suggests HF in adults, >400 pg/mL in children.
Shows ejection fraction, wall motion, valve function; EF <40% = systolic HF, EF 40‑50% with diastolic dysfunction.
Shows pulmonary vascular congestion, cardiomegaly; absence of infiltrates helps rule out pneumonia.
Detects arrhythmias, ischemia, LV hypertrophy; helps identify ischemic or valvular causes.

sections.p: NYHA class I–IV and ACC/AHA stages A–D guide prognosis and treatment intensity. Staging reflects functional limitation and structural progression.

t.b: Higher levels correlate with worse NYHA class.

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, rheumatic heart disease, HIV‑related cardiomyopathy, malaria, and anemia are common. In high‑income areas, ischemic heart disease dominates.

t.b: Identifies valve lesions (rheumatic) or coronary artery disease.
Anemia >10 g/dL can cause high‑output HF.
Elevated TSH suggests hypothyroidism; low TSH with high free T4 indicates hyperthyroidism.

sections.p: Patients feel breathlessness, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, edema, fatigue, and weight gain. Signs include crackles, jugular venous distension, and peripheral edema.
b: Dyspnea on exertion or at rest

t.b: Elevated JVP >8 cm H2O indicates right‑sided congestion.
Fine crackles at lung bases suggest pulmonary edema.

sections.p: Use a stepwise approach: basic labs, ECG, chest X‑ray, echocardiography, and BNP. When resources are limited, clinical assessment and bedside ultrasound are key.

t.b: Rapid assessment of ventricular size, wall motion, and pericardial effusion.

sections.p: Sudden worsening dyspnea, chest pain, syncope, or arrhythmias signal acute decompensation or ischemia. Complications include pulmonary edema, renal failure, and thromboembolism.

t.b: Pulmonary edema appears as Kerley B lines and alveolar infiltrates.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe dyspnea, chest pain, syncope, or arrhythmia

faq.a: Yes, severe anemia increases cardiac output, leading to high‑output heart failure.
They can worsen renal function and cause electrolyte imbalance; monitor kidney function and potassium.
Use clinical exam, BNP, and bedside ultrasound to estimate ventricular function.

exam: Explain the pathophysiology of systolic vs diastolic heart failure.
Describe the diagnostic workup for a patient with suspected CHF in a low‑resource setting.
Outline the first‑line pharmacologic therapy for chronic HF and justify each drug class.
